arXiv:1107.3191v2 [math.AP] 20 Jul 2011

On the wave-breaking phenomena and global existence for the generalized periodic Camassa-Holm equation

Guilong Gui Guilong GuiDepartment of Mathematics, Jiangsu University, Zhenjiang 212013, P. R. China
and The Institute of Mathematical Sciences, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shatin, Hong Kong Email address: glgui@amss.ac.cn , Yue Liu Yue LiuDepartment of Mathematics, University of Texas, Arlington, TX 76019-0408, USA Email address: yliu@uta.edu and Min Zhu Min ZhuDepartment of Mathematics, Nanjing Forestry University, Nanjing 210037, P. R. China
and Department of Mathematics, Southeast University, Nanjing 210097, P. R. China Email address: zhumin@njfu.edu.cn
Abstract.

Considered herein is the initial-value problem for the generalized periodic Camassa-Holm equation which is related to the Camassa-Holm equation and the Hunter-Saxton equation. Sufficient conditions guaranteeing the development of breaking waves in finite time are demonstrated. On the other hand, the existence of strong permanent waves is established with certain initial profiles depending on the linear dispersive parameter in a range of the Sobolev spaces. Moreover, the admissible global weak solution in the energy space is obtained.

Keywords: Generalized periodic Camassa-Holm equation, Wave-breaking, Global existence

AMS Subject Classification (2000): 35B30, 35G25

1. Introduction

We study here the initial-value problem associated with the generalized periodic Camassa-Holm (μ\mu-CH) equation [30], namely,

{μ(ut)−ux​x​t+2μ(u)ux+2κux=2uxux​x+uux​x​x,t>0,x∈ℝ,u(0,x)=u0(x),x∈ℝ,u(t,x+1)=u(t,x),t≥0,x∈ℝ,\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\begin{split}&\mu(u_{t})-u_{xxt}+2\mu(u)u_{x}+2\kappa u_{x}=2u_{x}u_{xx}+uu_{xxx},\quad t>0,\quad x\in\mathbb{R},\\ &u(0,x)=u_{0}(x),\qquad x\in\mathbb{R},\\ &u(t,x+1)=u(t,x),\quad\quad\quad t\geq 0,\quad x\in\mathbb{R},\end{split}\end{array}\right. (1.1)

where u⁡(t,x)u(t,x) is a time-dependent function on the unit circle 𝕊=ℝ/ℤ\mathbb{S}=\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z} and μ⁡(u)=∫𝕊u⁡(t,x)​𝑑x\mu(u)=\int_{\mathbb{S}}u(t,x)dx denotes its mean, the parameter κ∈ℝ\kappa\in\mathbb{R}. Obviously, if μ⁡(u)=0\mu(u)=0, which implies that μ⁡(ut)=0,\mu(u_{t})=0, then this equation reduces to the Hunter-Saxton (HS) equation [25], which is also a short wave limit of the Camassa-Holm (CH) equation [1, 5, 13, 23]. Equivalently, the initial value problem (1.1) can be rewritten as the following mixed hyperbolic-elliptic type system.

{ut+uux+∂xP=0,t>0,x∈ℝ,(μ−∂x2)P=2μ(u)u+12u2x+2κu,t>0,x∈ℝu(t,x+1)=u(t,x),t≥0,x∈ℝ,u(0,x)=u0(x),x∈ℝ.\begin{cases}u_{t}+uu_{x}+\partial_{x}P=0,\qquad t>0,\quad x\in\mathbb{R},\\ (\mu-\partial_{x}^{2})P=2\mu(u)u+\frac{1}{2}u^{2}_{x}+2\kappa\,u,\quad t>0,\quad x\in\mathbb{R}\\ u(t,x+1)=u(t,x),\quad\quad\quad t\geq 0,\quad x\in\mathbb{R},\\ u(0,x)=u_{0}(x),\qquad\qquad\qquad x\in\mathbb{R}.\end{cases} (1.2)

With m=(μ−∂x2)um=(\mu-\partial_{x}^{2})u, the first equation in (1.1) may be read as

mt+u​mx+2​m​ux+2​κ​ux=0.m_{t}+um_{x}+2mu_{x}+2\kappa u_{x}=0. (1.3)

It is known that the Camassa-Holm equation is one of the following family of equations with the parameter λ=2\lambda=2

mt+u​mx+λ​ux​m+2​κ​ux=0,m_{t}+um_{x}+\lambda u_{x}m+2\kappa u_{x}=0, (1.4)

with m=A​um=Au and A=1−∂x2A=1-\partial_{x}^{2}, the parameter κ∈ℝ\kappa\in\mathbb{R}. The family of equations are believed to be integrable [5, 17] only for λ=2\lambda=2 and λ=3\lambda=3.

It is observed that the μ\mu-CH equation is the corresponding μ\mu-version of the family given by (1.4) with m=A​um=Au, A=μ−∂x2A=\mu-\partial_{x}^{2}, and the parameter λ=2\lambda=2.

It is clear that the closest relatives of the μ\mu-CH equation are the Camassa-Holm equation with A=1−∂x2A=1-\partial_{x}^{2}

ut−ut​x​x+3​u​ux+2​κ​ux=2​ux​ux​x+u​ux​x​x,u_{t}-u_{txx}+3uu_{x}+2\kappa u_{x}=2u_{x}u_{xx}+uu_{xxx},

and the equation with A=−∂x2A=-\partial_{x}^{2}

−ut​x​x+2​κ​ux=2​ux​ux​x+u​ux​x​x.-u_{txx}+2\kappa u_{x}=2u_{x}u_{xx}+uu_{xxx}. (1.5)

It is noted that when κ=0\kappa=0, (1.5) becomes the Hunter-Saxton equation, while if κ≠0\kappa\neq 0, (1.5) is a short wave limit of the Camassa-Holm (CH) equation, which is an equation in the Dym hierarchy and admits a new class of soliton solutions(called umbilic solitons) [1].

Both of the CH equation and the HS equation have attracted a lot of attention among the integrable systems and the PDE communities. The Camassa-Holm equation was introduced in [5] as a shallow water approximation and has a bi-Hamiltonian structure [23], whose relevance for water waves was established in [13]. The Hunter-Saxton equation firstly appeared in [25] as an asymptotic equation for rotators in liquid crystals. Recently, it was claimed in [18] that the equation might be relevant to the modeling of tsunami, also see the discussion in [12].

The Camassa-Holm equation is a completely integrable system with a bi-Hamiltonian structure and hence it possesses an infinite sequence of conservation laws [5, 23], see [14] for the periodic case. When κ=0\kappa=0, it admits soliton-like solutions (called peakons) in both periodic and non-periodic setting [5] and the multi-soliton or infinite-soliton solutions consisting of a train of peaked solitary waves or ‘peakons’ [5, 6]. These peakons are weak solutions in the distributional sense and shown to be stable [6, 15, 16, 19, 20]. The Camassa-Holm equation describes geodesic flows on the infinite dimensional group 𝒟s​(𝕊){\mathcal{D}}^{s}(\mathbb{S}) of orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of the unit circle 𝕊\mathbb{S} of Sobolev class HsH^{s} and endowed with a right-invariant metric by the H1H^{1} inner product [31, 35]. The Hunter-Saxton equation also describes the geodesic flow on the homogeneous space of the group 𝒟s​(𝕊)\mathcal{D}^{s}(\mathbb{S}) modulo the subgroup of rigid rotations R​o​t​(𝕊)≃𝕊Rot(\mathbb{S})\simeq\mathbb{S} equipped with the H˙1\dot{H}^{1} right-invariant metric [32] at the identity

⟨u,v⟩H˙1=∫𝕊ux​vx​𝑑x.\langle u,v\rangle_{\dot{H}^{1}}=\int_{\mathbb{S}}u_{x}v_{x}dx.

The Hunter-Saxton equation possesses a bi-Hamiltonian structure and is formally integrable [26].

Another remarkable property of the Camassa-Holm equation is the presence of breaking waves (i.e. the solution remains bounded while its slope becomes unbounded in finite time [39]) [5, 8, 9, 10, 14, 34]. Wave breaking is one of the most intriguing long-standing problems of water wave theory [39]. It is worth pointing out that Bressan and Constantin proved that the solutions to the Camassa-Holm equation can be uniquely continued after wave-breaking as either global conservative or global dissipative weak solution in [2] and [3], respectively. It is noted that Xin and Zhang obtained the existence of a global-in-time weak solution to the Camassa-Holm equation in the energy space [41], where authors basically follow the approach in [45] to study the viscous approximate solutions to the Camassa-Holm equation.

The μ\mu-CH was introduced by Khesin, Lenells and Misiolek [30] (also called μ\mu-HS equation). Similar to the HS equation [25], the μ\mu-CH equation describes the propagation of weakly nonlinear orientation waves in a massive nematic liquid crystal with external magnetic filed and self-interaction. Here, the solution u⁡(t,x)u(t,x) of the μ\mu-CH equation represents the director field of a nematic liquid crystal, xx is a space variable in a reference frame moving with the linearized wave velocity, and tt is a slow time variable. Nematic liquid crystals are fields consisting of long rigid molecules. The μ\mu-CH equation is also an Euler equation on 𝒟s​(𝕊)\mathcal{D}^{s}(\mathbb{S}) (the set of circle diffeomorphism of the Sobolev class HsH^{s}) and it describes the geodesic flow on 𝒟s​(𝕊)\mathcal{D}^{s}(\mathbb{S}) with the right-invariant metric given at the identity by the inner product [30]

⟨u,v⟩=μ⁡(u)​μ​(v)+∫𝕊ux​vx​𝑑x.\langle u,v\rangle=\mu(u)\mu(v)+\int_{\mathbb{S}}u_{x}v_{x}dx.

It was shown in [30] that the μ\mu-CH equation is formally integrable and can be viewed as the compatibility condition between

ψx​x=ξ⁡(m+κ)​ψandψt=(12​ξ−u)​ψx+12​ux​ψ,\psi_{xx}=\xi(m+\kappa)\psi\quad\mbox{and}\quad\psi_{t}=\left(\frac{1}{2\xi}-u\right)\psi_{x}+\frac{1}{2}u_{x}\psi,

where ξ∈ℂ\xi\in\mathbb{C} is a spectral parameter and m=μ⁡(u)−ux​xm=\mu(u)-u_{xx}.

On the other hand, the μ\mu-CH equation admits bi-Hamiltonian structure and infinite hierarchy of conservation laws. The first few conservation laws in the hierarchy are

H0=∫𝕊m​𝑑x,H1=12​∫𝕊m​u​𝑑x,H2=∫𝕊(μ⁡(u)​u2+κ​u2+12​u​ux2)​𝑑x.H_{0}=\int_{\mathbb{S}}m\ dx,\quad H_{1}=\frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathbb{S}}mu\ dx,\quad H_{2}=\int_{\mathbb{S}}\left(\mu(u)u^{2}+\kappa\,u^{2}+\frac{1}{2}uu_{x}^{2}\right)dx.

It is noted that the Hunter-Saxton equation does not have any bounded traveling-wave solutions at all, while the μ\mu-CH equation admits traveling waves that can be regarded as the appropriate candidates for solitons. It is shown in [30, 33] that when κ=0\kappa=0, the μ\mu-CH equation admits not only periodic one-peakon solution u⁡(t,x)=φ⁡(x−c​t)u(t,x)=\varphi(x-ct) where

φ⁡(x)=c26​(12​x2+23)\varphi(x)=\frac{c}{26}(12x^{2}+23)

for x∈[−12,12]x\in[-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}] and φ\varphi is extended periodically to the real line, but also the multi-peakons of the form

u=∑i=1Npi​(t)​g​(x−qi​(t)),u=\sum^{N}_{i=1}p_{i}(t)g(x-q_{i}(t)),

where g⁡(x)=12​x​(x−1)+1312g(x)=\frac{1}{2}x(x-1)+\frac{13}{12} is the Green function of the operator (μ−∂x2)−1(\mu-\partial_{x}^{2})^{-1}.

Note that Hs↪L​i​pH^{s}\hookrightarrow Lip for s>32s>\frac{3}{2}. From the theory of the transport equation point of view, one may define a strong solution to (1.2) as follows.

Definition 1.1.

If u∈C⁡([0,T),Hs​(𝕊))∩C1​([0,T),Hs−1​(𝕊))u\in C([0,T),H^{s}(\mathbb{S}))\cap C^{1}([0,T),H^{s-1}(\mathbb{S})) with s>32s>\frac{3}{2} satisfies (1.2), then uu is called a strong solution to (1.2). If uu is a strong solution on [0,T)[0,T) for every T>0T>0, then it is called global strong solution to (1.2).

One of our goals in this paper is concerned with the existence of a global weak solution in the energy space H1H^{1}, which is motivated by the work in [41].

Definition 1.2.

A continuous function u=u⁡(t,x)u=u(t,x) is said to be an admissible global weak solution to the initial-value problem (1.2) if

(i) u⁡(t,x)∈C⁡(ℝ+×𝕊)∩L∞​(ℝ+,H1​(𝕊))u(t,x)\in C(\mathbb{R}^{+}\times\mathbb{S})\cap L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{+},H^{1}(\mathbb{S})) and

μ⁡(u)=μ⁡(u0)and‖∂xu⁡(t,⋅)‖L2​(𝕊)≤‖∂xu0​(⋅)‖L2​(𝕊)∀t>0;\mu(u)=\mu(u_{0})\quad\mbox{and}\quad\|\partial_{x}u(t,\cdot)\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{S})}\leq\|\partial_{x}u_{0}(\cdot)\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{S})}\quad\forall\quad t>0; (1.9)

(ii) u⁡(t,x)u(t,x) satisfies the equations in (1.2) in the sense of distributions and takes on the initial data pointwise.

Our main results of the present paper are Theorems 3.1- 3.4 (wave-breaking), Theorems 4.1-4.2(Global strong solution), and Theorem 5.1(Global weak solution).

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, some a priori estimates and basic properties on its strong solutions to the μ\mu-CH equation are recalled and derived, which are constantly used in the whole paper. In Section 3, the results of blow-up to strong solutions are established in details. It is shown that the solutions of the μ\mu-CH equation can only have singularities which correspond to wave breaking (Theorems 3.1-3.4). Two sufficient conditions for the existence of global strong solutions (Theorems 4.1-4.2) are specified in Section 4. The existence of an admissible global weak solution in the energy space H1H^{1} (Theorem 5.1) is demostrated in the last section, Section 5.

Notations. Throughout this paper, we identity all spaces of periodic functions with function spaces over the unit circle 𝕊\mathbb{S} in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}, i. e. 𝕊=ℝ/ℤ\mathbb{S}=\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}. Since all space of functions are over 𝕊\mathbb{S}, for simplicity, we drop 𝕊\mathbb{S} in our notations of function spaces if there is no ambiguity. For a given Banach space ZZ, we denote its norm by ∥⋅∥Z\|\cdot\|_{Z}.

2. Preliminaries

In the following, we establish some a priori estimates for the μ\mu-CH equation. Recall that the first two conserved quantities of the μ\mu-CH equation are

H0=∫𝕊m​𝑑x=∫𝕊(μ⁡(u)−ux​x)​𝑑x=μ⁡(u⁡(t)),H_{0}=\int_{\mathbb{S}}m\ dx=\int_{\mathbb{S}}\left(\mu(u)-u_{xx}\right)dx=\mu(u(t)),

and

H1=12​∫𝕊m​u​𝑑x=12​μ2​(u⁡(t))+12​∫𝕊ux2​(t,x)​𝑑x.H_{1}=\frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathbb{S}}mu\ dx=\frac{1}{2}\mu^{2}(u(t))+\frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathbb{S}}u^{2}_{x}(t,x)dx.

It is easy to see that μ⁡(u⁡(t))\mu(u(t)) and ∫𝕊ux2​(t,x)​𝑑x\int_{\mathbb{S}}u^{2}_{x}(t,x)dx are conserved in time [30]. Thus

μ⁡(ut)=0.\mu(u_{t})=0.

For the sake of convenience, let

μ0=μ⁡(u0)=μ⁡(u⁡(t))=∫𝕊u⁡(t,x)​𝑑x\mu_{0}=\mu(u_{0})=\mu(u(t))=\int_{\mathbb{S}}u(t,x)dx (2.1)

and

μ1=(∫𝕊ux2​(0,x)​𝑑x)12=(∫𝕊ux2​(t,x)​𝑑x)12.\mu_{1}=\left(\int_{\mathbb{S}}u^{2}_{x}(0,x)dx\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}=\left(\int_{\mathbb{S}}u^{2}_{x}(t,x)dx\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}. (2.2)

Then μ0\mu_{0} and μ1\mu_{1} are constants and independent of time tt.

5. Existence of global weak solution

In this section, we establish the existence of an admissible global weak solution to (1.2), which may be stated as follows.

Theorem 5.1.

Assume that u0∈H1​(𝕊)u_{0}\in H^{1}(\mathbb{S}). Then the initial-value problem (1.1) has an admissible global weak solution, u=u⁡(t,x)u=u(t,x), in the sense of Definition 1.2. Furthermore, this weak solution u⁡(t,x)u(t,x) satisfies the following properties.

(i) One-sided supernorm estimate: There exists a positive constant C=C⁡(u0)C=C(u_{0}) such that the following one-sided L∞L^{\infty} norm estimate on the first-order spatial derivative holds in the sense of distribution:

∂xu⁡(t,x)≤1t+C,∀t>0,x∈𝕊.\partial_{x}u(t,x)\leq\frac{1}{t}+C,\quad\forall\quad t>0,\,x\in\mathbb{S}. (5.1)

(ii) Space-time higher integrability estimate.

∂xu∈Ll​o​cp​(ℝ+×𝕊),∀ 1≤p<3,\partial_{x}u\in L^{p}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}^{+}\times\mathbb{S}),\quad\forall\,1\leq p<3,

i.e., for any 0<T<+∞0<T<+\infty, there exists a positive constant C1=C1​(T,p)C_{1}=C_{1}(T,p) such that

∫0T∫𝕊|∂xuε​(t,x)|p​𝑑x​𝑑t≤C1,∀ 1≤p<3.\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{S}}|\partial_{x}u_{\varepsilon}(t,x)|^{p}\,dx\,dt\leq C_{1},\quad\forall\,1\leq p<3. (5.2)

The proof of this theorem is motivated by the one of Theorem 1.2 in [41]. This method, as far as we know, was first used by Zhang and Zheng to study an admissible global solution to a variational wave equation in [45].

In this subsection, we drive the theory of Young measures (see Lemma 4.2 in [41], also [42], [43],[44], [46]) to obtain the necessary compactness of the viscous approximate solution uε​(t,x)u_{\varepsilon}(t,x). We first state a compactness lemma.

([38]) Let XX, BB, YY be three Banach spaces and satisfy X↪↪B↪YX\hookrightarrow\hookrightarrow B\hookrightarrow Y, 1≤p≤∞1\leq p\leq\infty, T>0T>0. Assume that a set FF of functions ff is bounded in Lp​([0,T],X)L^{p}([0,T],X) and satisfies that

Then FF is relatively compact in Lp​([0,T],B)L^{p}([0,T],B) (and in C⁡([0,T],B)C([0,T],B) if p=∞p=\infty).

We are in a position to prove that the Young measure μt,x​(λ)\mu_{t,x}(\lambda) is a Dirac measure.

5.4. Proof of Theorem 5.1

Proof of Theorem 5.1.

With all the preparations given in the previous subsection, we are in a position to conclude the proof of the theorem. Let u⁡(t,x)u(t,x) be the limit of the viscous approximate solutions uε​(t,x)u_{\varepsilon}(t,x) as ε→0+\varepsilon\rightarrow 0^{+}. It then follows from Propositions 5.1, 5.2 and 5.4 that u⁡(t,x)∈C⁡(ℝ+×𝕊)∩L∞​(ℝ+,H1​(𝕊))u(t,x)\in C(\mathbb{R}^{+}\times\mathbb{S})\cap L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{+},H^{1}(\mathbb{S})), Π⁡(t)∈L∞​(ℝ+)\Pi(t)\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{+}) and (1.9) (5.1) hold.

Now we claim that

qε=∂xuε→q=∂xuasε→0+inLl​o​c2​(ℝ+×𝕊).q_{\varepsilon}=\partial_{x}u_{\varepsilon}\rightarrow q=\partial_{x}u\quad\mbox{as}\quad\varepsilon\rightarrow 0^{+}\quad\mbox{in}\quad L^{2}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}^{+}\times\mathbb{S}). (5.50)

Indeed, it follows from (5.31) and Lemma 5.7 that there exists a subsequence of {uε​(t,x)}\{u_{\varepsilon}(t,x)\}, still denoted by itself, such that

qε=∂xuε→q=∂xuinLl​o​cp1​(ℝ+,Lp2​(𝕊))∀p1<∞,p2<2.q_{\varepsilon}=\partial_{x}u_{\varepsilon}\rightarrow q=\partial_{x}u\quad\mbox{in}\quad L^{p_{1}}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}^{+},L^{p_{2}}(\mathbb{S}))\quad\forall\quad p_{1}<\infty,\quad p_{2}<2.

This together with Proposition 5.3 and a standard interpolation theorem applied implies

qε=∂xuε→q=∂xuinLl​o​cp​(ℝ+×𝕊)∀p<3,q_{\varepsilon}=\partial_{x}u_{\varepsilon}\rightarrow q=\partial_{x}u\quad\mbox{in}\quad L^{p}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}^{+}\times\mathbb{S})\quad\forall\quad p<3, (5.51)

which gives (5.50).

Thus, we get from (5.29) and (5.6) that Π⁡(t)=μ⁡((∂xu)2)\Pi(t)=\mu((\partial_{x}u)^{2}).

Taking ε→0+\varepsilon\rightarrow 0^{+} in (5.3), one finds from (5.50) and Proposition 5.4 that uu is an admissible weak solution to (1.2). It then follows from (5.51) that ∂xu∈Ll​o​cp​(ℝ+×𝕊)\partial_{x}u\in L^{p}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}^{+}\times\mathbb{S}) for any 1≤p<31\leq p<3. Hence the local space-time higher integrability estimate (5.2) holds. This completes the proof of Theorem 5.1. ∎
